title: Simpsonville takes shape on the Louisville road
summary: In Shelby County, Isaac Watkins petitioned to lay out Simpsonville in 1816 as a waystation on the Louisville–Shelbyville road. A post office opened in 1821; the town…
bodyMarkdown:
Simpsonville sits in western Shelby County, about 8 miles west of [Shelbyville](/stories/shelbyville/) and 23 miles east of Louisville on today's U.S. 60. [Simpsonville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simpsonville,_Kentucky) was laid out in 1816 on the petition of Isaac Watkins. It got its first post office in 1821 and was incorporated in 1833.

## The man behind the name

The town was named for Capt. John Simpson. [John Simpson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Simpson_%28Kentucky_politician%29) was born in Virginia and came to Kentucky with his family as a child in the 1780s. He volunteered for Gen. Anthony Wayne's Legion during the Northwest Indian War. He was present for the campaign that ended at Fallen Timbers in 1794, but he stayed behind to guard supplies and did not fight in the battle.

Simpson then moved to Shelby County, studied law and became one of its first attorneys. He served four terms in the Kentucky House from 1806 to 1811 and was Speaker from 1810 to 1811. In 1812 he won a seat in Congress, but the War of 1812 began before he took office, and he rejoined the army.

He was killed at the [River Raisin](/stories/river-raisin-1813-kentuckys-winter-defeat-in-michigan/) on January 22, 1813. Simpson County is also named for him.

## A stagecoach town

By 1825 Simpsonville had become one of the largest stagecoach stops between Shelbyville and Louisville. Coaches on the Midland Trail changed or rested their horses there, and travelers could stay at the Old Stone Inn. The inn is the second-oldest stone building in the county still standing.

For most of its history, Simpsonville was a farming community. Dairy, tobacco, cattle and hogs were the main sources of income, helped by fertile limestone soil.

## The 1865 ambush

In January 1865, at least 80 men of Company E, 5th U.S. Colored Cavalry, were driving 900 head of federal cattle from [Camp Nelson](/stories/camp-nelson-kentucky-us-colored-troops/) to Louisville. On the morning of January 25, Confederate guerrillas led by Henry Magruder attacked their camp at Simpsonville from the rear. They killed 22 Union soldiers and wounded more than 20, and at least some were killed after trying to surrender.

No one was ever prosecuted for the attack. Magruder was later convicted by a military tribunal for other murders and executed in Louisville on October 20, 1865.

## Lincoln Institute

After Kentucky's Day Law barred Berea College from teaching Black students, Berea built the Lincoln Institute near Simpsonville. The boarding school for African American students opened in 1912 and offered high school and vocational classes. It closed in 1966 as enrollment fell after Brown v. Board of Education.

## Kentucky today

Simpsonville had 2,990 people in 2020. The town calls itself the "American Saddlebred Horse Capital of the World." Interstate 64, finished in 1965, links it to Louisville, and it is a short drive from [Bagdad](/stories/bagdad-how-a-shelby-county-rail-stop-took-over-consolation/).
